# Parallel Numerics Bench

**Reproducible serial/parallel accuracy and scaling - an original C++17
thread pool with deterministic workloads, equivalence tests and honest
multi-repeat timings.**

[![CI](https://github.com/khalil-official/parallel-numerics-bench/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/khalil-official/parallel-numerics-bench/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-1f4e79.svg)](LICENSE)

![Monte Carlo pi convergence animation](docs/results/mcpi_convergence.gif)

*Animation provenance: generated by `scripts/make_gif.py` from
`docs/results/progress.csv`, recorded on 2026-10-18 by
`pnb_bench --mode progress` (serial run, 60 checkpoints x 1,000,000 fresh

i5-12500H described below. Each of the 60 frames is one recorded
checkpoint at its actual sample count - nothing interpolated or
synthesized. Final recorded estimate: 3.14166.*

## Purpose and scope

Parallel numerical code has two failure modes that benchmarks usually hide:
**answers that drift when you add threads**, and **speedup tables that
cherry-pick the good cells**. This project is a small, complete,
from-scratch answer to both:

* a **header-only `ThreadPool`** (condition-variable worker queue,
  `enqueue` returning `std::future`) written from scratch - standard
  textbook design, ~100 lines, no dependencies beyond the C++17 standard
  library;
* two **deterministic numerical workloads** built on it - Monte Carlo pi
  estimation with an original **counter-based RNG** (samples addressed by
  `(stream, counter)`, split by stream so serial and parallel code use the
  identical sample set), and a blockwise dense **matrix product**;
* **serial reference implementations** and machine-checked equivalence
  claims that state exactly what is bit-identical and what is only
  tolerance-close, and why;
* a **measurement driver** with a written methodology: >= 7 repeats per
  cell (8 kept + 1 discarded cold run by default), median and min,
  serial/parallel cells interleaved round by round, full scatter plotted,
  sub-unity "speedups" reported as-is.

Scope limits up front: shared memory only (no MPI/GPU/distributed), no
NUMA or affinity claims, timings are machine-specific (hardware string in
every results file), and the RNG is statistical - not cryptographic, not
BigCrush-certified (details in [docs/verification.md](docs/verification.md)).

## Quick start

```bash
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release   # GCC/Clang/MSVC, C++17
cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure       # 9 test executables
./build/pnb_bench --mode smoke                   # tiny end-to-end sanity run
```

Reproduce the measurements (CSVs land in `docs/results/`):

```bash
./build/pnb_bench --mode scaling      # timed sweep, bench.csv
./build/pnb_bench --mode equivalence  # serial vs parallel sweep, equivalence.csv
./build/pnb_bench --mode progress     # 60-checkpoint MC run, progress.csv

pip install -r scripts/requirements.txt   # matplotlib + pillow (plotting only)
python scripts/plot_results.py --cpu "your CPU here"   # figures + tables + summary
python scripts/make_gif.py                             # animation from progress.csv
```

The workloads are pure C++; Python touches only the recorded CSVs.
Warning policy: `-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic` (`/W4` on MSVC), CI builds with
`-Werror`.

## Architecture

```
src/thread_pool.hpp    ThreadPool: workers + condition_variable + task queue;
                       enqueue -> std::future (values and exceptions)
src/counter_rng.hpp    counter-based RNG: sample(stream, counter) = mixed64 of
                       both; stream splitting; raw-counter negative control
src/workloads.hpp      partitioning helpers, shared block kernels, serial and
                       parallel variants of both workloads + input validation
src/timing.hpp         Stopwatch (steady_clock), median/min statistics
src/bench_main.cpp     measurement driver: scaling / equivalence / progress /
                       smoke modes, CSV + environment recording
tests/                 9 CTest executables (pool, RNG statistics, partition,
                       equivalence x2, determinism, validation, timing, headers)
scripts/               plot_results.py, make_gif.py (consume CSVs only)
docs/                  model.md (math + methodology), api.md,
                       verification.md (evidence + limits), results/
```

The determinism contract in one paragraph (full version in
[docs/model.md](docs/model.md)): the unit of work is a contiguous block;
the partitioning is a pure function of (n, blocks); ONE shared kernel
computes a block, called once by the serial reference and once per task by
the parallel path, so scheduling cannot change any bit. MC hit counts are
integers - exact, associative, bit-identical under ANY partitioning. Every
matrix element is a fixed-order dot product - C is bit-identical under any
row-block partitioning. The floating checksum is merged from block
partials and is deliberately claimed only tolerance-close (measured <=
7.3e-15 relative, bit-identical at 1 thread) because floating addition is
not associative - but its merge order is fixed, so it is still
bit-stable across reruns.

## Measured results (this machine, this run)

Full table: [docs/results/speedup_table.md](docs/results/speedup_table.md)
- scatter of every repeat: [docs/results/scaling.png](docs/results/scaling.png)
- machine record: [docs/results/run_summary.json](docs/results/run_summary.json).

Context: Intel i5-12500H (12 cores: 8P+4E, 16 logical), Windows 11,
GCC 16.2.0 Release, medians of 8 kept repeats (cold run discarded,
serial/parallel cells interleaved round by round).

| Workload | Size | Serial median | 16-thread median | Speedup | Honest note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monte Carlo pi | 5,000,000 | 93.8 ms | 10.0 ms | **9.36x** | near-linear to 8 P-cores, then hyper-threads |
| Matrix product | 768 | 1.506 s | 0.237 s | **6.35x** | compute-bound naive kernel |
| Monte Carlo pi | 100,000 | 1.66 ms | 0.33 ms | 5.08x | small size still scales, but see the 1-worker row |
| Monte Carlo pi | 100,000 (1 worker) | 1.66 ms | 2.11 ms | **0.79x** | pool dispatch SLOWER than serial at ~ms scale - reported as measured |
| Matrix product | 96 (1 worker) | 1.12 ms | 1.32 ms | **0.85x** | same overhead story, reported as measured |

Also read in the table: threads=1 cells at larger sizes show up to ~1.1x
"speedup" over serial - both paths run the identical kernel, so that is
CPU frequency-state drift between interleaved cells on this power-limited
laptop, not a parallel effect; speedups should be read from threads >= 2.

Equivalence (24 recorded cells, `docs/results/equivalence.csv`):
MC hit counts and matrix C **bit-identical in every cell**; parallel reruns
bit-stable in every cell; checksum relative deltas 0 (1 thread) to
7.3e-15 (16 threads) - the documented non-associativity, plotted in
[docs/results/equivalence_deltas.png](docs/results/equivalence_deltas.png).

## Verification summary

* **9/9 CTest suites pass**: pool semantics (futures, exception
  propagation, drain-on-destroy, exact task counts), RNG statistics
  (determinism, chi-square equidistribution, pairwise stream correlation,
  lag-1 autocorrelation of a merged interleaved stream, overlapping-window
  test, plus a raw-counter negative control that must FAIL), partition
  invariants, serial/parallel equivalence for both workloads across sizes
  and thread counts, cross-run determinism, input validation, timing
  statistics.
* In-run determinism: every repeat of every bench cell produced an
  identical result string (`run_summary.json` flag:
  `bench_results_bit_stable_across_repeats: true`).
* CI: Ubuntu + Windows matrix, CMake build + CTest + smoke run
  ([.github/workflows/ci.yml](.github/workflows/ci.yml)).

Per-test evidence and the exact limits of every claim:
[docs/verification.md](docs/verification.md).

## Limitations

Shared-memory single-machine parallelism only; no NUMA/affinity/pinning
claims; timings are specific to one laptop and one session (record your
own with the commands above); the RNG is a statistical generator whose
tested properties are exactly those listed in
[docs/model.md](docs/model.md) - nothing more is claimed; the matrix kernel
is a reference kernel (no blocking/SIMD tuning), so absolute matmul times
are not a FLOPS claim.

## References (by title)

* *C++ Concurrency in Action* (Anthony Williams) - the condition-variable
  thread pool and packaged_task/future patterns this project implements
  from scratch.
* *The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 2: Seminumerical Algorithms*
  (Donald E. Knuth) - chi-square equidistribution testing and the theory
  behind counter/mixing constructions.
* *Random Number Generation and Monte Carlo Methods* (James E. Gentle) -
  stream splitting and parallel RNG design.
* *What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point
  Arithmetic* (David Goldberg) - non-associativity of floating addition,
  the reason the checksum claim is tolerance-level only.
